item.title: After School Arts Programs Are a Win-Win for Students and Parents
item.description: I wasn’t the next Bob Ross or anything, but the club kept me engaged and out of trouble.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Karl

item.title: Singapore Can Fix Southeast Asia’s Haze, If It Wants To
item.description: A cloud of haze has descended across Southeast Asia over the past few months as a brutal El Niño helps incinerate forest and scrub in Indonesia. Obscuring responsibility for the fires stems from a much deeper and more impenetrable legal pall.
item.dc:creator: David Fickling

item.title: Starbucks Can Sell China, Not the China Risk
item.description: Starbucks Corp.’s decision to revive its business in China by giving up majority control to a local partner looks increasingly like an astute way of operating when commercial pressure and political risk collide.
item.dc:creator: Juliana Liu

item.title: Don’t Bet Against the Sports Bets
item.description: Also parking-lot data centers, BDC arbitrage, Hood Summit and Midnight Madness.
item.dc:creator: Matt Levine

item.title: Free Universal After-School Would Help Kids, Parents and the Economy
item.description: It’s a time-honored tradition for one generation to shake its head at the next, wondering if progress and technology have caused more harm than good. So it is now, with some prominent academics saying kids today need to be off their screens or unsupervised more often, as they were in simpler times.
item.dc:creator: Kathryn Anne Edwards

item.title: Florida Governor Race: Byron Donalds Personifies GOP Emptiness
item.description: When students at Florida A&M University in Tallahassee grilled Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds last month about his record, he promised to bring his finance background to the state’s top job. “The next governor has to have experience in how a company’s balance sheet operates,” said Donalds, who was a financial adviser before being elected to the Florida House in 2016 and the US House in 2020.
item.dc:creator: Mary Ellen Klas

item.title: Robinhood’s AI Agents Won’t Help You Beat the Market
item.description: We are all investors now, or at least the majority of us are. More Americans than ever are investing in the stock market, and surveys show a large share of Gen Z and millennials actively trade individual stocks as their preferred investment strategy. Most people lose money or underperform with this latter endeavor. But take a bull run and technology that makes trading feel like a video game, and suddenly, everyone thinks they can beat the market.
item.dc:creator: Allison Schrager

item.title: Congress: Just Say Yes to Common-Sense Permitting Reform
item.description: After decades of debate and innumerable false starts, Congress may be on the cusp of a major overhaul of America’s broken permitting system. Few reform efforts of recent years have been so dull — or quite so consequential. Both parties should get on board.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: Meta’s Muse Is Ending Its Honeymoon Phase on Solid Ground
item.description: You can barely take a step on the New York subway lately without seeing the face of Meta Platforms Inc.’s furry Muse AI assistant. I’ve written already about how impressed I’ve been with the form and function of the breakthrough bot. Now, attention must move to assessing whether Muse has long-term staying power — or whether its launch will be just a flash in the pan.
item.dc:creator: Dave Lee

item.title: Trump’s Energy Midterms Will Be Worse Than Biden’s
item.description: Four years ago, Americans were reeling from painfully high pump prices and pundits warned the incumbent government would face a protest wave in midterm elections. Sound familiar?
item.dc:creator: Liam Denning

item.title: Rising Bond Yields Are No Substitute for Tighter Monetary Policy
item.description: Are the bond and derivatives markets doing the tough work for central bankers? Swaps are pricing a globally coordinated cycle of interest rate increased over the next 12 months, and longer-term bond yields are hitting multi-decade highs in the US, Europe and Japan. item.dc:creator: Jonathan Levin

item.title: We Should Worry More About English Girls' Education
item.description: The UK, for all its political instability and sluggish growth, recently got some good news: British students ranked in the top 10 across all tested subjects in the latest results from the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). The UK was one of just eight countries to achieve that feat — 92 countries and cities participated — and also managed to buck wider downward trends by improving its average science score and avoiding a decline in reading.
item.dc:creator: Lara Williams

item.title: Why Putin Says Russia Could “Cease to Exist” If It Loses in Ukraine
item.description: Ever since things in Ukraine first went sideways for Vladimir Putin back in the spring of 2022, the Russian president and his officials have said that, not only were they fighting Nazis and responding to NATO aggression, but that the stakes of the conflict were so high that Russia may cease to exist should they fail.
item.dc:creator: Marc Champion

item.title: Big Oil Goes Back to Iraq for Contracts Amid Iran War
item.description: “Buy to the sound of cannons, sell to the sound of trumpets.” The ancient stock market maxim resonates in today’s Middle East. While the US and Iran fight, Big Oil is heading into neighboring Iraq.
item.dc:creator: Javier Blas

item.title: Britain’s Richest People Have a New Champion: Kemi Badenoch
item.description: “Blessed are the rich,” is an unlikely credo for a modern British politician, but Tory leader Kemi Badenoch dared to speak up for the highly taxed, affluent professional classes in her Conservative Party conference speech last week.
item.dc:creator: Martin Ivens
